Analysis Pipeline: Per-row median subtraction for row alignment (median is robust to blobs) -> VERIFY streak removal: extract line profiles perpendicular to fast-scan over featureless regions; if residual row-to-row offset or streaks remain, ESCALATE to per-row 1st-2nd order polynomial subtraction and re-verify -> resample to square pixels using metadata FOV (512x512 no-op; 256x512 upsample slow axis to 512x512 assuming square FOV; record nm/px via resolve_pixel_size_nm; fall back to cyc/px with explicit caveat if calibration unavailable), preserving true aspect ratio -> fourier_reflection_map on the leveled square-pixel image -> ARTIFACT REJECTION: reject any detected reflection whose orientation is aligned with the residual streak axis (i.e. a horizontal-streak-induced vertical-frequency ridge) unless it independently passes the null-gate AND spot_snr_domain > spot_snr_bulk AND the domain map corresponds to real image content (not edge/streak bands) -> compare spacing, sigma, domain_fraction, spot_snr_domain vs spot_snr_bulk between 2 mM and 10 mM; report 'no resolvable order' as a legitimate finding for 10 mM if criteria are not met.

Quality Status: All analyses acceptable

1. Scientific Analysis

This series aims to characterize how the surface structure/adsorbate pattern on mica evolves between 2 mM and 10 mM KCl using AFM height maps. Two frames were analyzed with a rigorous, artifact-aware pipeline (per-row median leveling escalated to polynomial subtraction, streak-removal verification, square-pixel resampling, fourier_reflection_map with strict streak-axis artifact rejection and null/SNR/coherence gating). Both frames passed quality verification (scores 0.79 and 0.87, mean 0.83), and streak removal was fully successful in the 2 mM frame (streak_std reduced from ~1341 to ~4e-12 after escalation to polynomial leveling). The critical finding is that the intended comparative analysis is essentially UNRESOLVED, because only the 2 mM frame produced extractable quantitative features. The 10 mM entry has empty extracted_features and quality_metrics, so no spacing, domain fraction, SNR, or reflection-count values are available for it. Consequently the 'trend' between concentrations is degenerate: every feature is reported as a single point with no regression possible. For the 2 mM frame, the pipeline detected 28 candidate reflections and a nominal periodicity of ~0.392 nm at a frequency of ~0.498 cyc/px, with a high sigma-resolvability (7.65). However, this reflection was NOT confirmed as real ordered-adsorbate/lattice content: reflection_present is False, the domain SNR (14.5) is substantially LOWER than the bulk SNR (34.7), so spot_snr_domain_gt_bulk is False and reflection_confirmed_domain_gt_bulk is False. The domain fraction is very small (~0.025, i.e. ~2.5% of the field). A frequency of ~0.498 cyc/px is essentially at the Nyquist limit (0.5 cyc/px), which is a classic signature of a pixel-grid / single-pixel-alternation artifact rather than genuine surface periodicity. Combined with the fallback pixel calibration (100 nm FOV assumption, 0.195 nm/px), the '0.392 nm' spacing is an artifact of the Nyquist frequency times an assumed pixel size, not a physically meaningful lattice constant. The gating logic correctly declined to confirm this as a real reflection. Taken together, the data support a conservative conclusion: at 2 mM KCl, no resolvable, spatially-coherent ordered-adsorbate lattice reflection is confirmed above bulk background, and at 10 mM no quantitative features were extractable at all. The comparative objective (how structure changes from 2 to 10 mM) therefore cannot be answered from the present dataset; the most defensible statement is that neither frame provides confirmed evidence of an ordered adsorbate superlattice under these imaging/calibration conditions.

5. Scientific Claims

Claim 1: At 2 mM KCl on mica, no ordered-adsorbate/lattice reflection is confirmed above bulk background: the leading Fourier candidate (~0.498 cyc/px, i.e. at the Nyquist limit) has lower domain SNR (14.5) than bulk SNR (34.7) and occupies only ~2.5% of the field, failing the domain>bulk confirmation gate.

Scientific Impact: Establishes a rigorous null result and prevents over-interpretation of near-Nyquist Fourier peaks as genuine atomic/adsorbate lattices, which is a common pitfall in high-resolution AFM of electrolyte-mica interfaces.

Literature Search Query: Has anyone rigorously distinguished genuine ordered-adsorbate lattice reflections from Nyquist-limit pixel-grid artifacts in AFM height maps of the KCl–mica interface using domain-vs-bulk SNR gating?

Keywords: AFM, mica, KCl, Fourier analysis, Nyquist artifact, ordered adsorbate, null result

6. Caveats & Limitations

The comparative objective cannot be answered: only 1 of 2 frames yielded quantitative features (the 10 mM frame is empty), so no true concentration trend can be established — all 'trends' are single-point and degenerate. Pixel calibration relied on a fallback 100 nm FOV assumption, so the reported 0.392 nm spacing is not metrologically reliable; its frequency (~0.498 cyc/px) sits at the Nyquist limit, a strong indicator of a pixel-grid artifact rather than a real lattice. The single detected candidate at 2 mM failed the domain>bulk SNR gate (14.5 < 34.7) and occupies only ~2.5% of the field, so no confirmed ordered structure exists even at 2 mM. With only two concentrations and no replicates, statistical confidence is minimal. Conclusions should be limited to (a) a conservative null at 2 mM and (b) a data-completeness failure at 10 mM requiring re-analysis with explicit null reporting and true scale metadata before any concentration-dependence claim is made.
